issues.legal_issue: A court’s jurisdiction to reconsider an administrative decision is appellate in nature when it has plenary power to review and alter that decision, even if the governing provision describes the proceeding as an application rather than an appeal.
material_facts: An aggrieved person applied to the District Court to set aside the Charity Commissioner’s decision concerning whether properties belonged to a public trust.
The District Court could confirm, revoke, or modify the Commissioner’s decision, and could reconsider the matter on law and fact without fetters or limits on that power.
issues.conclusion: The District Court exercised appellate jurisdiction when deciding the application; the absence of the word “appeal” in the provision did not change the nature of the jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: The nature of a proceeding depends on its substance, scope, and content, rather than its label. The Court applied Section 72(1) and (2) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, and approved Hiragar Dayagar v. Ratanlal, [1972] 13 G.L.R. 181, and the reasoning in (1956) 58 Bombay Law Reporter 894. It disapproved AIR 1974 Bombay 40.

predicates.application_seeks_review_of_administrati: An aggrieved person asks a court to reconsider an administrative decision.
predicates.reviewing_court_can_reconsider_merits: The court can review the merits of the decision, including questions of law and fact.
predicates.reviewing_court_can_alter_decision: The court can confirm, modify, revoke, or set aside the decision.

issues.definition: When an aggrieved person asks a court to review an administrative decision and the court can reconsider its merits and alter it, the court exercises appellate jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A further appeal under the governing appellate procedure requires the prescribed leave when a single judge hears an appeal from a decision made by a court exercising appellate jurisdiction and subject to the High Court’s superintendence.
material_facts: The District Court’s decision on the application was made in the exercise of appellate jurisdiction.
A single judge of the High Court heard an appeal from that decision.
The appellant filed a Letters Patent Appeal without obtaining the required certificate from the single judge.
issues.conclusion: Clause 15 of the Letters Patent applied, and the Letters Patent Appeal was not maintainable without the required certificate; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 15 of the Letters Patent of Bombay requires the prescribed leave for an appeal from a single judge’s decision in a matter arising from the appellate jurisdiction of a court subject to the High Court’s superintendence. The Court relied on its holding that the District Court’s jurisdiction under Section 72 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, was appellate.

predicates.further_appeal_from_single_judge_decisio: A party seeks a further appeal from a single judge’s decision.
predicates.single_judge_decision_concerns_district_: The single judge’s decision concerns an order made by a District Court exercising appellate jurisdiction.
predicates.district_court_subject_to_high_court_sup: The District Court whose order is at issue is subject to the High Court’s superintendence.
predicates.required_leave_not_obtained: The party seeking the further appeal has not obtained the required leave from the single judge.

issues.definition: A further appeal is not maintainable when it challenges a single judge’s decision concerning an appellate order of a District Court subject to High Court superintendence and the required leave was not obtained.
